items.title: Change the ports SightPress uses
items.text: A port is a numbered door on your computer that a program listens on. Each address SightPress uses ends in a port number, such as the 8080 in http://localhost:8080. If another program already uses one of these ports, SightPress can't start and you see an error such as "port is already allocated". This guide shows you how to choose different ports.

items.title: The ports SightPress uses
items.text:
Setting Default What it is for HTTP_PORT 8080 SightPress itself MAILPIT_UI_PORT 8025 The test e-mail inbox MAILPIT_SMTP_PORT 1025 Where the test e-mail inbox receives e-mail MINIO_API_PORT 9000 File storage MINIO_CONSOLE_PORT 9001 The file storage console

The error message names the port that is taken, for example 127.0.0.1:8080.

items.title: Change a port
items.text:
1. If SightPress is running, stop it. See Run SightPress in the background, or press Ctrl+C in the terminal where it runs.

  2. In the skeleton folder, check whether a file called .env exists. If it doesn't, create it by copying the example file:

    cp .env.example .env

    On Windows in PowerShell, cp works too.

  3. Open .env in a text editor, such as Notepad on Windows or TextEdit on macOS. The name starts with a dot, so some file browsers hide it; you can open it from the editor's Open menu instead.

  4. Find the line for the port you want to change, for example HTTP_PORT=8080, and change the number, for example to HTTP_PORT=8081. Pick a number between 1024 and 65535 that no other program uses.
  5. Save the file.
  6. Start SightPress again with docker compose up.
  7. Use the new number in the address. With HTTP_PORT=8081, go to http://localhost:8081. You should see the No site configured page.

items.title: Who can reach these ports
items.text: Every port listens only on your own computer (the address 127.0.0.1, also called localhost). Other computers on your network can't reach SightPress.

items.title: Codes we send you
items.text:
A SightPress website never sends you a link to click. When it needs to check that an e-mail address is yours, it sends a 6-digit code instead, and you type that code on the website yourself.

This keeps you safe from fake messages. If you ever get a message that claims to come from a SightPress website and asks you to click a link, it is not from us. Don't click it.

items.title: When you get a code
items.text:
You get a code by e-mail when:

  • you forgot your password and asked for a new one: the code works for 15 minutes;
  • someone invited you to help with a website: the invitation code works for 7 days.

The person who sets up a new website gets a setup code from the command line tool, not by e-mail. They pass it on to the website's first admin, who uses it to choose a password. A setup code works for 7 days.

Each code works only once.

items.title: What a code message looks like
items.text:
• The subject names the website, for example "Your code to reset your password for Riverside Library" or "Ada invited you to Riverside Library". The code itself is never in the subject.
  • The message has the code on its own line, for example 123 456.
  • The message has no links, no web addresses and no pictures.
  • It ends with: "We will never send you a link. Type this code on the page where you asked for it. Never share it with anyone."

items.title: Type a code
items.text:
1. Go to the page that asked for the code. For a password, that is the page you are already on. For an invitation, go to the website's sign-in page and choose Accept an invitation.
  2. Find the field called 6-digit code.
  3. Type the 6 digits. You can type them with or without the space in the middle.
  4. Choose Continue. The page never sends the code by itself, so take your time.
  5. You should see the next step, for example a page where you choose your password.

items.title: If the code doesn't work
items.text:
• Check the digits and try again. After 5 wrong tries the code stops working.
  • A code also stops working when it is too old, when it has been used, or when you asked for a newer one.
  • On the password page, choose Send a new code. You can ask for a new code once a minute; if it is too soon, the page tells you how many seconds to wait.
  • For an invitation, ask the person who invited you to invite you again.
  • For a setup code, ask the person who set up the website for a new one.

items.title: Try it on your computer
items.text: When SightPress runs on your computer, the e-mails with codes go to the test inbox. See Open the test e-mail inbox.

items.title: Create a website
items.text:
One SightPress installation can run many websites. Each website has its own pages, people, files and settings, kept in its own database. This guide shows you how to create a website with the command line tool, and what each part of the command means.

Before you start, follow Getting started up to step 6, so that SightPress runs and has a secret key.

items.title: Create the website, answering questions
items.text:
The easiest way is to let the command ask you everything, one question at a time.

  1. Open a terminal and go to the skeleton folder.

  2. Type:

    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:create

  3. Answer each question and press Enter. Each question says what to type. When it ends with "Press Enter for" and a value, pressing Enter without typing takes that value. When it lists choices, such as "Type person or organization", type one of them; capital letters don't matter.

  4. For the database, the command first asks which engine to use. Press Enter for SQLite: it keeps the website in one file and needs nothing else. Press Enter again to keep the file in the sites folder. If you choose MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL instead, the command asks for the server, port, database name, user name and password one by one, each with a usual value you can keep with Enter. The password isn't shown as you type it, and you type it twice so a typing mistake is caught.
  5. For the main language, type a code such as en-GB or pt-BR. Capital letters don't matter and you can use _ instead of -. The command says the language in words, for example "That is Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR). Is that right?". Type yes or press Enter if it is, or no to type it again.
  6. If an answer isn't right, for example an e-mail address without the part after @, the command says what is wrong and asks again. After 3 wrong answers in a row it stops and creates nothing; just start again.
  7. At the end, the command lists all your answers, one per line, and asks "Is all of this right?". Press Enter to create the website. Type no to go through the questions again: your answers are kept, so press Enter for each one that was right and type only what you want to change.
  8. You should see one sentence for each thing SightPress did, ending with: The site "demo" is ready at https://localhost. On your own computer, the address to open is http://localhost:8080: answer http://localhost:8080 to the question "Address the site is opened at".
  9. One of the sentences gives the setup code for the first admin, for example: "Give the setup code 388 641 to ada@example.org." Give the code to that person in a way you trust, such as in person or by phone. SightPress doesn't e-mail it.
  10. The first admin goes to the address in that sentence (for example http://localhost:8080/login/setup), types their e-mail address and the code, and chooses a password. Step 8 of Getting started shows each screen.

items.title: Create the website with one command
items.text:
If you already know every answer, for example in a script, give them all on one line. The command then asks nothing. This example creates a website called "Riverside Library" for an organisation:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:create demo --domain=localhost --db-engine=sqlite --url=http://localhost:8080 --owner-type=organization --locale=en-GB --name="Riverside Library" --admin-email=ada@example.org --admin-first-name=Ada --admin-last-name=Lovelace

If something is wrong, the command says what, and creates nothing.

items.title: What each part means
items.text:
Part What to give Example demo A short name for the website: lower-case letters, digits and hyphens. You use it in other commands. library --domain The web addresses of the website, without https://, separated by commas. Each address belongs to one website only. On your own computer, use localhost. library.example.org,www.library.example.org --db-engine The database engine: sqlite, mysql, mariadb or postgresql. On your own computer, SQLite is simplest. See Start a database server for the others. sqlite --db-path For SQLite: the file. Optional: without it, a file named after the short name in the sites folder. library.sqlite --db-host, --db-port, --db-name, --db-user, --db-password For the other engines: the server, its port, the database, and the user name and password. Without them, localhost, the engine's usual port, sightpress_ and the short name, sightpress and no password. --db-host=db --db-user=library --db Instead of the parts above: the whole database address in one go. sqlite:////app/sites/library.sqlite --owner-type Who runs the website: organization or person, in capitals or not. The ready-made pages say "we" for an organisation and "I" for a person. person --locale The website's main language. Capital letters don't matter, and _ works as well as -. en-GB, pt_br, fr-FR --name The name visitors see. Optional: without it, the short name is used. "Riverside Library" --admin-email, --admin-first-name, --admin-last-name The first admin of the website. ada@example.org --timezone Optional. The time zone for dates on the website. Europe/London --url Optional. The address printed with the setup code. Without it, SightPress prints https:// and the first domain. On your own computer, use http://localhost:8080. http://localhost:8080 --create-db Optional. Creates the database on a MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL server if it doesn't exist yet. --with-demo-content Optional. Adds demo pages, files and people for trying SightPress out. Don't use it for a real website.

Put quotation marks around anything with spaces, such as the website's name.

items.title: What a new website has
items.text:
Every new website starts ready to use:

  • six published pages: a home page called "Welcome to" and the website's name, About, Contact (with a contact form whose messages go to the first admin), a privacy notice, terms of use and an accessibility statement;
  • a main menu with About and Contact, and a footer menu with the other three pages;
  • a logo, an icon and a picture for sharing on social media, made from the website's name;
  • the roles admin, editor, contributor and member (see Roles and permissions).

The ready-made pages are in English, whatever the website's language. Change or translate them in the admin panel.

items.title: Try SightPress with demo content
items.text:
Add --with-demo-content to the command to fill the new website with examples:

  • five files in the media library: a picture, a short video with captions, a sound recording and a PDF;
  • a page called "Every kind of block" at /every-block, with one block of every kind, and a page under it;
  • three more people, each waiting for their setup code: Bea Okafor (editor), Cleo Martins (contributor) and Max Müller (member).

The command prints a setup code for each person. The example.org addresses can't receive e-mail, so give the codes to whoever tries the website out.

items.title: Give someone a new setup code
items.text:
A setup code works once, for 7 days. To make a new one for an admin who hasn't chosen a password yet, type:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:user:create-admin demo --email=ada@example.org --first-name=Ada --last-name=Lovelace --url=http://localhost:8080

You should see a new setup code. The old one stops working. The same command adds another admin when you give a new e-mail address. Someone who already has a password uses Forgot your password? on the sign-in page instead.

items.title: Turn a website off, or remove it
items.text:
To Type Visitors see turn it off for a while bin/sightpress site:disable demo "temporarily unavailable" turn it on again bin/sightpress site:enable demo the website close it and keep its data bin/sightpress site:archive demo "gone" delete it, softly bin/sightpress site:delete demo "not found"; the data is kept remove a deleted website for good bin/sightpress site:purge demo —

Start each command with docker compose run --rm --no-deps php, as above. site:purge keeps the database unless you add --drop-database, which can't be undone. The command line reference lists every command.

items.title: Fix upload size limits
items.text: How large a file you can upload depends on two things: what the website accepts for each kind of file, and what the server accepts in one go. This guide explains the warning admins see when the server's settings are too low, and how to change them.

items.title: What you see
items.text:
• Next to the upload field in Media, everyone sees the largest file they can upload, for example "Largest file you can upload: pictures 20 MB, documents 50 MB, audio files 64 MB and videos 64 MB."
  • If you choose a file that is too large, the browser refuses it before sending it. The reason appears under the field, which gets focus, so screen readers read it out.
  • If something too large is sent anyway, you see a page called This is too large to send. It says how much the server accepts and has a Go back to the form link.
  • Admins see a warning called Your server’s settings stop some uploads on the dashboard and in Media. Each point names a server setting and the value it needs. Editors and contributors don't see it.

items.title: Change the limits on your own computer
items.text:
With SightPress running in Docker, the limits are one group of lines in the .env file of the skeleton folder. PHP and the web server both read them, so they always match.

  1. If there is no .env file in the skeleton folder yet, create it by copying the example:

    cp .env.example .env

  2. Open .env in a text editor and find the lines that start with UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE.

  3. Change the values you need:

    Setting Recommended What it is UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE 64M The largest file in one upload INPUT_MAX_SIZE 8M The largest form without files, such as a long page INPUT_MAX_VARS 5000 How many fields one form can have; lower values can lose content MAX_FILE_UPLOADS 20 How many files one upload can hold PHP_MEMORY_LIMIT 256M Memory for one request; 512M for pictures over 25 million pixels UPLOAD_TIMEOUT 300 Seconds a slow upload may take

    Sizes are whole megabytes or gigabytes, such as 64M or 1G. On a small site or shared hosting, 32M is enough for UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE.

  4. Save the file and restart SightPress:

    docker compose up -d

  5. Check the result:

    docker compose exec php bin/sightpress system:check

    You should see the limits, the largest file of each kind, and No problems found. If something is still wrong, it is listed with the setting to change.

If a value is not valid, for example UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE=lots, SightPress doesn't start and the terminal says which value to fix.

items.title: On a hosting provider's server
items.text: If someone else runs your server, send them the warning's text. It names the settings, for example upload_max_filesize, post_max_size or the web server's limit (client_max_body_size for nginx), and the value each needs. Ask them to tell you when it is done, then open the dashboard again: the warning is gone once the settings are right.

items.title: Large audio files and videos
items.text: The website accepts audio files up to 200 MB and videos up to 1 GB, but for now one upload can't be larger than UPLOAD_MAX_SIZE. A later version will send large files in parts, so they can be larger than the server's limit. system:check mentions this as a note, not a problem.

items.title: Open the file storage console
items.text:
SightPress comes with a file storage program called MinIO, which has its own web console. This guide shows you how to sign in to it.

  1. Start SightPress (see Getting started).
  2. In your web browser, go to http://localhost:9001.
  3. You should see the MinIO sign-in page.
  4. Sign in with the user name sightpress and the password sightpress-secret.
  5. You should see the MinIO console. There are no files yet.

In this version, websites don't use MinIO yet. Each website keeps its uploaded files, such as pictures and documents, in its own folder inside the sites folder of the skeleton. A later version will let websites store their files in MinIO or another storage service.

If you changed MINIO_ROOT_USER, MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD or MINIO_CONSOLE_PORT in your .env file, use your values instead. These settings only take effect the first time the storage starts.

items.title: Open the test e-mail inbox
items.text:
When SightPress runs on your computer, it never sends real e-mail. Every message goes to a test inbox called Mailpit instead, so you can read it without anything leaving your computer. This guide shows you how to open it.

  1. Start SightPress (see Getting started).
  2. In your web browser, go to http://localhost:8025.
  3. You should see the Mailpit inbox. It is empty for now, with a message saying there are no messages.

SightPress sends e-mail when:

  • someone forgets their password and asks for a code;
  • someone is invited to help with a website;
  • a page is sent for review: every editor and admin is told;
  • a visitor sends a message with a contact form.

Each of these messages appears here a moment later. Choose a message to read it.

The inbox only gets messages when your .env file has the line MAILER_DSN=smtp://mailpit:1025. The file you copied from .env.example in Getting started already has it. Without it, SightPress sends nothing.

If you changed MAILPIT_UI_PORT in your .env file, use that number instead of 8025.

items.title: Run SightPress in the background
items.text: In Getting started, SightPress runs in a terminal window and stops when you close it. This guide shows you how to run it in the background instead.

items.title: Start SightPress
items.text:
1. Open a terminal and go to the skeleton folder, for example:

    cd sightpress/skeleton

  2. Type:

    docker compose up --detach --wait

  3. Wait until the command finishes. You should see one line per container (php, nginx, mailpit and minio), each ending with Healthy. You get your terminal back.

  4. Go to http://localhost:8080. You should see the No site configured page.

    The very first time, SightPress keeps installing for a minute or two after the command finishes, and the browser shows 502 Bad Gateway. Wait a minute, then reload the page.

You can now close the terminal. SightPress keeps running until you stop it or restart your computer.

items.title: See what is running
items.text:
Type:

docker compose ps

You should see a table with one row for each container. The STATUS column says Up and how long the container has been running.

items.title: Read the messages SightPress writes
items.text:
Type:

docker compose logs --follow

You see the messages from every container, and new ones as they arrive. Press Ctrl+C to stop reading. SightPress keeps running.

items.title: Stop SightPress
items.text:
Type:

docker compose --profile "*" down

You should see lines ending with Removed. The --profile "*" part also stops a database server if you started one. Your settings and stored files are kept for next time.

Shortcuts for macOS and Linux

If the make program is installed, you can type make up to start SightPress in the background and make down to stop it. Type make on its own to list every shortcut.

items.title: Search your website
items.text: Every page of a website has a search box in its header. It finds the website's published pages in the language you are reading, by their title, their summary and their text, including the descriptions of pictures, the transcripts of recordings and the names of downloads. Site search is an optional feature, on by default.

items.title: Search from any page
items.text:
1. Open any page of your website, for example http://localhost:8080/.
  2. In the header, find Search this site. With a keyboard, press Tab until you reach the search box.
  3. Type one or more words, for example opening hours, and press Enter (or choose Search).
  4. You should see the results page. Its title and heading say what you searched for and how many results there are, for example "2 results for “opening hours”". Screen readers read this out when the page opens.
  5. Each result has its title as a link, where it is on the website ("In: About us › Team") and a few lines of its text with the words you searched for in bold and underlined. Choose a title to open the page.

Good to know:

  • Capitals and accents don't matter: cafe finds "Café".
  • Words are matched by their stem: libraries finds "library".
  • The last word can be the start of a word: accessib finds "accessibility".
  • Pages with every word come first. When no page has every word, the results page says so and shows pages with some of them.
  • With ten results or more, links at the bottom ("Search results pages") lead to the next pages.

items.title: When nothing is found
items.text: The page says "No results for …" and gives tips: check the spelling, try fewer or other words. On a website in several languages, the language list at the top leads to the same search in the other languages.

items.title: Pages for members only
items.text: Pages for members only are found only by people who are signed in. Sign in, search again, and they appear in the results.

items.title: Leave a page out of the search
items.text:
1. Open the page in the admin panel's page editor.
  2. In the Search & AI section, tick Leave this page out of the site’s own search.
  3. Choose Save.
  4. Check: searching for the page's title no longer finds it. Search engines can still list the page, unless you also tick Ask search engines and AI search engines not to list this page.

The choice is made for each language of the page.

items.title: If new pages don't show up
items.text:
The search follows every change as it is saved. After a bigger change (adding a language, changing the website's main language, making the whole website members-only, or turning search back on), SightPress rebuilds the search within a minute, as long as it runs in the background (see Run SightPress in the background). To rebuild it straight away, in the skeleton folder type (replace demo with your website's short name):

docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:search:reindex demo

You should see one line per language, such as en-GB: 12 documents indexed.

items.title: Turn search off
items.text: Search is a feature: an admin can turn it off on the Features screen (see Turn features on or off). The search box and the results page are then gone.

items.title: See who visits your website
items.text:
SightPress counts how many people visit your website, which pages they read, where they come from, what they search for and which addresses are not found. It also shows which search engines and AI crawlers read the website. Analytics is an optional feature, on by default.

It is private by design: visits are counted on your own server, with no cookies, no tracking scripts and nothing sent to other companies. SightPress never stores visitors' IP addresses or details of their browser. This is not legal advice, but it means most websites don't need a cookie banner for it.

items.title: Open the Analytics screen
items.text:
1. Sign in to the admin panel as an admin or an editor, for example at http://localhost:8080/admin.
  2. In the admin menu, choose Analytics. (Contributors don't have it.)
  3. You should see the last 30 days. Under Days to show, the link for the range you are looking at is marked as the current one; choose Last 7 days, Last 90 days or Last 12 months to change it.
  4. For other dates, fill in First day and Last day under Other days and choose Show these days. If a date is missing or the last day comes before the first, a box at the top says "There is a problem" and links to the field to fix.

Days run from midnight to midnight in your website's time zone, which the screen names, so everyone sees the same numbers. Today's numbers are counted live.

items.title: Read the numbers
items.text:
At the top, three sentences sum up the range, for example "1,349 visitors, up 12% on the 30 days before". The arrows next to them are only decoration: the words say the same.

Each part of the screen has its own heading, so a screen reader can move between them:

  • Visitors over time: a chart, with a sentence above it that says what it shows, for example "Visitors went up 12% compared with the previous 30 days, from 1,204 to 1,349. The busiest day was Tuesday 4 November, with 98 visitors." This period is a solid line with round markers, the period before a dashed line with square markers. Choose Show the data for each day to see every day in a table.
  • Pages read most, Where visitors came from and Devices (phone, tablet or computer): tables, with a small bar next to each number.
  • Languages: only on websites in more than one language.
  • Site search: what people searched for, and the searches that found nothing. Only while site search is on. Searches that look like an email address or a phone number are counted but never shown.
  • Pages not found: addresses people asked for that don't exist. People who can edit any page see Add a redirect next to each one: it opens the Redirects screen with the address filled in.
  • Search engines and AI crawlers: which programs read the website and what they read. They are never counted as visitors.

Each part has a Download … as a CSV file link, for a spreadsheet. The file has every row, not only the first ten.

items.title: What is counted and what isn't
items.text:
• A visitor is counted once per day. The same person on two days counts twice; there is no "returning visitors" number, on purpose.
  • Not counted: people signed in to the website, visitors whose browser asks websites not to track them (Global Privacy Control or Do Not Track), the admin panel, pictures and other files, and pages a browser only loads in advance.
  • Figures are kept for 25 months, so you can compare two full years.

items.title: The dashboard
items.text: The dashboard (/admin) shows Last 7 days: one sentence with the visitors and page views of the last week, and a link to the Analytics screen.

items.title: Keep analytics for less time, or delete them (admins)
items.text:
1. On the Analytics screen, go to Keeping analytics at the bottom.
  2. In Months to keep analytics for, type a number from 1 to 25 and choose Save. Older figures are deleted within the hour. The change is in the audit log.
  3. To delete everything, choose Delete analytics data. A page asks you to confirm; choose Delete analytics data again, or Keep the data to go back. Counting goes on from then.

items.title: From the command line
items.text:
In the skeleton folder (replace demo with your website's short name):

docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:analytics:report demo

You should see the visitors, page views and views per visitor of the last 30 days, each with the 30 days before. Add --report=pages (or sources, devices, not-found …) for another report, and --format=csv or --format=json for a file. If it warns that analytics were "last rolled up" long ago, SightPress isn't running in the background (see Run SightPress in the background).

items.title: Turn analytics off
items.text: Analytics is a feature: an admin can turn it off on the Features screen (see Turn features on or off). Nothing is counted any more, and the figures already counted are kept until they are deleted. If your website's Privacy notice page was written by SightPress, remove its "Visitor statistics" section.

items.title: Start a database server
items.text:
SightPress keeps its data in a single file on disk (an SQLite database), so it doesn't need a separate database server. If you want to try one, SightPress can start MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL for you. This guide shows you how.

Not used yet

At this stage SightPress starts the database server but doesn't store anything in it. You can check that it runs. Later versions will let you use it for your sites.

items.title: Start SightPress with a database
items.text:
1. If SightPress is running, stop it with docker compose --profile "*" down.

  2. In the skeleton folder, type one of these commands:

    docker compose --profile mysql up

    For MariaDB, use --profile mariadb. For PostgreSQL, use --profile postgres.

  3. Wait until the text stops scrolling. The first time, Docker downloads the database, which can take a few minutes. You should see lines starting with mysql-1 (or mariadb-1, or postgres-1) among the others.

To start it in the background instead, add --detach --wait to the end of the command.

items.title: Check that the database runs
items.text:
1. Open a second terminal and go to the skeleton folder.

  2. Type:

    docker compose --profile "*" ps

  3. You should see a row for the database, such as mysql, with (healthy) in the STATUS column. If it says (health: starting), wait a few seconds and type the command again.

When you start SightPress without --profile, no database server runs, and this table has no database row.

items.title: The database settings
items.text:
The database is created with these values. You can change them in the .env file before the first start (see Change the ports SightPress uses for how to create and edit .env).

Setting Default What it is DB_NAME sightpress The name of the database DB_USER sightpress The user name DB_PASSWORD sightpress The user's password DB_ROOT_PASSWORD sightpress-root The administrator password (MySQL, MariaDB)

The database server can only be reached by the other SightPress containers, not from your computer or your network.

items.title: Stop the database
items.text: Type docker compose --profile "*" down. This stops SightPress and the database. The data in the database is kept for next time.

items.title: Try the command line tool
items.text: SightPress has a command line tool for tasks such as creating a website. This guide shows you how to run it.

items.title: List the commands
items.text:
1. Open a terminal and go to the skeleton folder.

  2. Type:

    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress list

  3. You should see a list of commands, each with one line about what it does, such as site:create Creates a site: its database, its first admin and its roles.

items.title: List your websites
items.text:
1. Type:

    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:list

  2. You should see one sentence for each website, with its status, its addresses, its language and its database. If you haven't created a website yet, it says "There are no sites yet. Create one with site:create."

items.title: Get help with one command
items.text:
1. Type help and the name of the command, for example:

    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress help site:create

  2. You should see what the command needs and what each option means.

To create a website, see Create a website. The command line reference lists every command.

Shortcut for macOS and Linux

If the make program is installed, make site-create NAME=demo runs site:create demo and asks for the rest.

items.title: Turn features on or off
items.text:
Some parts of SightPress are optional features, for example site search or visitor statistics. Each website has its own: an admin can turn a feature off for one website and keep it on for the others. Turning a feature off hides everything it adds, on the website and in the admin panel, and keeps its data, so turning it on again brings it back as it was.

You need to be an admin of the website. Editors, contributors and members don't see the Features screen.

Optional features in this version

This version of SightPress has three optional features of its own: Site search (see Search your website), Analytics (see See who visits your website), both on for new websites, and the AI assistant (see Use the AI assistant), off for new websites. Features installed as extra packages show up on the screen too.

items.title: See the features of a website
items.text:
1. Sign in to the admin panel of the website, for example http://localhost:8080/admin.
  2. In the admin menu, choose Features.
  3. You should see one section for each optional feature, with its name as a heading, what it does, its Status ("On" or "Off") and what happens when it is off.

A feature that says "set by your organisation" was chosen for every website by whoever runs your SightPress installation. It has no button, and it can't be changed from the website.

items.title: Turn a feature off
items.text:
1. On the Features screen, find the feature and choose Turn off followed by its name, for example Turn off Events.
  2. A page asks you to confirm and says what will happen. Choose Turn off … again to go ahead, or Keep … on to go back without changing anything.
  3. You are back on the Features screen, at the feature's heading. A message at the top says that it is off and that its data is kept. Screen readers read the message out.
  4. Check: the pages the feature added now answer "not found", and its screens have left the admin menu.

If another feature needs this one, SightPress refuses and names that feature: turn that one off first.

items.title: Turn a feature on
items.text:
1. On the Features screen, choose Turn on followed by the feature's name.
  2. You are back at the feature's heading, with the message "… is on."
  3. Check: its pages and screens are back, with the data they had before.

If the feature needs another feature that is off, SightPress refuses and names the feature to turn on first.

items.title: Delete a feature's data
items.text:
This removes everything the feature stored for the website, for good. You can only do it while the feature is off.

  1. Turn the feature off (see above).
  2. Under the feature, choose Delete the data of …. The link only appears when there is data to delete.
  3. A page asks you to confirm. Choose Delete the data of … to go ahead, or Keep the data to go back.
  4. The message says the data was deleted. Turning the feature on again later starts afresh, with no data.

Every change on this screen is written to the website's Audit log, with who made it and when.

items.title: With the command line tool
items.text:
The same can be done in a terminal, in the skeleton folder. Replace demo with the short name of your website and acme.events with the feature's id, which the first command shows.

  1. List the features of a website and whether each one is on:

    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:module:list demo

  2. Turn one on, or off:

    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:module:enable demo acme.events
docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:module:disable demo acme.events

  3. Turn one off and delete its data for good:

    docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress site:module:disable demo acme.events --purge-data

When you create a website, site:create demo --without=acme.events starts it with that feature off.

items.title: For whoever runs the installation
items.text:
In config/tenant.php, the modules section changes the features of every website:

  • defaults says which features new websites start with, for example 'defaults' => ['analytics' => false]. Websites that already exist keep what they have.
  • locked turns a feature on or off for every website, for example 'locked' => ['analytics' => false]. Admins then see "set by your organisation" and can't change it, and neither can the command line tool.

items.title: Use the AI assistant
items.text:
The AI assistant suggests text for your website: summaries, descriptions for search engines, alt text for pictures, drafts of pages and translations. It also answers questions about using SightPress. It uses an AI service you choose, with your own key from that service, so you pay the service directly for what you use.

The assistant only ever suggests. Nothing it writes is used until a person inserts it and saves. Alt text and translations it writes are marked until a person has checked them, and pages that use them can't be published before that.

The AI assistant is an optional feature, off for new websites. Nothing is sent to any AI service until an admin sets it up and someone asks for a suggestion.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• You need to be an admin of the website to turn the assistant on and set it up.
  • You need an API key from one of the AI services SightPress works with: Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (GPT), Mistral AI, or a service or your own server that works like OpenAI's. Each service's website explains how to get a key and what it costs. Check where the service processes data before you choose it: Mistral AI, for example, processes it in the EU.

items.title: Turn the assistant on
items.text:
1. Sign in to the admin panel, for example at http://localhost:8080/admin.
  2. In the admin menu, choose Features.
  3. Find AI assistant and choose Turn on AI assistant.
  4. You should see that its status is now "On". A new screen appears in the admin menu under Site settings: AI assistant.

See Turn features on or off for more about features.

items.title: Choose the service and enter your key
items.text:
1. In the admin menu, choose Site settings, then AI assistant.
  2. Under Status you should see "Not ready yet", followed by what is missing.
  3. Under AI service, choose a service. Each one says what it is.
  4. Choose a Model. Bigger models write better and cost more. For an OpenAI-compatible service, type the Model name and the Address of the service instead (it must start with https://).
  5. Paste your key into New API key and choose Save the AI service.
  6. You should see "The AI service is saved." Under Status it now says "Ready", and the page shows only the last four characters of your key, for example "Saved API key: ••••1234". The key is stored encrypted and never shown again. To change it, paste a new one; to delete it, choose Remove key.
  7. Choose Test connection. You should see "The connection works", or what went wrong (for example a key the service didn't accept).

If your organisation chooses the AI service for every website, this screen shows its choice and you can't change it.

items.title: Choose who may use it, and a budget
items.text:
1. On the same screen, under Who may use it, and how much, tick the roles that may ask the assistant. Admins always may.
  2. In Monthly budget in tokens, enter how many tokens (pieces of words, sent and received) the website may use each month. Leave it empty to use your organisation's budget; enter 0 for no limit.
  3. Choose Save who may use it. The screen shows how much has been used this month.

Months start on the 1st. From 80% of the budget, everyone who asks is warned; at 100% the assistant stops until the next month. Each person can ask 20 times every 10 minutes.

items.title: Ask a question
items.text:
1. On the Dashboard (or at the end of a page's editor), find Ask the assistant.
  2. Type your question in Your question, for example "How do I add a page to the main menu?", and choose Ask.
  3. You should hear or see "Working on it…", then "Suggestion ready". The answer appears under its own heading, which gets focus. It ends with a link to the part of this documentation it used.

The assistant only tells you about screens your role can use. If something needs an admin, it says so.

On a page's editor you can tick Share this page with the assistant to ask about the page itself. It reads the saved page, so save your changes first.

items.title: Get a suggestion for a field
items.text:
On a page's editor, under Summary, Title in search results and Description for search engines, there is a Suggest button.

  1. Save the page first: the assistant reads the saved page.
  2. Choose, for example, Suggest a summary.
  3. The suggestion appears in Ask the assistant, under its own heading, which gets focus.
  4. Choose Insert to put it in the field (focus goes back to the field), Copy to copy it, Try again for another one, or Discard.
  5. Check the text, change it if needed, and choose Save page.

Without JavaScript, the same buttons open a page with the suggestion; Insert takes you back to the field with the text in it.

items.title: Rewrite text, draft a page, or explain a check
items.text:
• Rewrite text (in every Ask the assistant): paste some text, choose Make it simpler, shorter, friendlier or more formal, and choose Rewrite. Copy the result into your page.
  • Draft this page (on a page's editor): say what the page should be about and choose Draft this page. Choose Add to the end of the page: the headings and text are added to the page's blocks, not yet saved. Things to check or fill in are in [square brackets].
  • Explain this (next to each publish check on a page's editor): the assistant explains what the check means and how to fix it.

items.title: Alt text for pictures
items.text:
The assistant can describe pictures only with a model that can see pictures (most listed models can).

  1. In the admin menu, choose Media and open a picture.
  2. Under the alt text field, choose Suggest alt text.
  3. Choose Insert, check the text, and choose Save details.
  4. You should see "The AI assistant suggested this alt text." Pages that show this text can't be published until someone checks it.
  5. When the text describes the picture well, tick I checked the alt text: it describes the picture and choose Save details. Changing the text and saving it counts as checking it too.

items.title: Draft a translation
items.text:
On a website in more than one language:

  1. Open a page's editor. In the Translations section, choose Draft a translation into followed by the language, with the AI assistant.
  2. The new translation opens in the editor, with a notice: "The AI assistant drafted this translation, and nobody has checked it yet." Its blocks, pictures and links are the same as the original's; only the words are translated.
  3. Read it and change what needs changing. Then save the page, or choose I checked this translation.
  4. Only then can the translation be published. Until then the list of pages and the page's older versions say "drafted by the AI assistant, not checked yet".

items.title: What is sent, and what is kept
items.text:
• Sent to the AI service: your question, and the page or picture you ask a suggestion for. Never lists of people, email addresses, the audit log or other pages.
  • Kept on your website: when the assistant was used, by whom, for what, with which service and model, and how many tokens. Never the question, the page text or the answer.
  • The AI service handles what it receives under its own terms.

items.title: Turn the assistant off
items.text: On the Features screen, choose Turn off AI assistant. The panel, the Suggest buttons and the AI assistant screen disappear. The settings, the key and the record of what was used are kept, so turning it on again brings everything back.

items.title: From the command line
items.text: Whoever runs your SightPress installation can set the assistant up with site:assistant:set, test it with site:assistant:test, see what was used with site:assistant:usage and turn it off with site:assistant:disable. See the command line reference.

items.title: Write and publish a page
items.text:
This guide shows you how to start a page, add its content, and take it through review until visitors can read it. Every step works with a keyboard alone and with a screen reader.

You need an account on the website with the role contributor, editor or admin. See Roles and permissions.

items.title: Start a page
items.text:
1. Sign in to the website, for example at http://localhost:8080/login. You should see the Dashboard.
  2. Choose Pages in the admin menu, then Start a new page. You should see the heading Start a new page.
  3. In Title, type the page's title, for example Book club. You can change it later.
  4. In Put it under, choose where the page belongs. Choose None: a top-level page for a page of its own, or another page to put it under that one. A page under "About us" gets an address such as /about/book-club.
  5. Leave Layout on Standard page. Home page shows the title and summary as a large introduction.
  6. Choose Start the page. You should see the message "“Book club” has been started as a draft. Add its content, then save it." and the heading Edit “Book club”.

A new page is a draft: nobody else sees it until it is published.

items.title: Add the content
items.text:
A page is made of blocks, shown one after another: a heading, some text, a picture and so on. The blocks reference describes every kind.

  1. Go to the Content section. On a new page it says "There are no blocks yet. Add the first one below."
  2. In Type of block to add, choose a kind of block, for example Text.
  3. Choose Add block. You should hear or see "Added a Text block. It is block 1 of 1. Save the page to keep this change." Focus moves to the new block, a group called "Block 1 of 1: Text".
  4. Fill in the block's fields. For a Text block, type your text in Text. You can use simple HTML, such as <p>We meet every first <strong>Tuesday</strong> of the month.</p>. Update the previews shows how it will look.
  5. Add more blocks the same way. Each block has the buttons Move up, Move down and Remove. After each one, you hear or see what changed, for example "Moved block 2 (Text) up. It is now block 1 of 2." Focus stays on the block or on the button.
  6. Choose Save page. It is at the top and at the bottom of the form; pressing Enter in a field saves too. You should see "Saved “Book club”."

The block buttons don't save

Adding, moving and removing blocks changes the form only. Nothing is kept until you choose Save page.

If the page can't be saved, a list of problems appears at the top of the page and gets focus. Each problem is a link to the field it is about, for example "Heading text: Fill in this field." Fix it and save again.

items.title: Help people find the page
items.text:
The Search & AI section decides how the page looks in search engines, in AI search and when it is shared. All its fields are optional, but a description and a summary help people find the page.

  • Summary: one or two sentences about the page. Shown in lists of pages and read by AI search engines.
  • Title in search results: only when it should differ from the page title.
  • Description for search engines: one or two sentences. Search engines show about 160 characters. A count of the characters is read out after a short pause.
  • Ask search engines and AI search engines not to list this page: tick it to keep the page out of search results. It is then also left out of the sitemap and llms.txt.

How a search result could look shows the title, the address and the description as text. Choose Update the previews after a change. Search and AI visibility explains the rest.

items.title: Check the page before you send it
items.text:
Under the form, SightPress checks the saved page:

  • Problems that stop publishing, for example a picture without alt text, a video without captions or a heading that skips a level. A page with these can't be published until they are fixed.
  • Suggestions, for example "Add a description for search engines". The page can be published with these.

Each item links to the field or block it is about. When there are only suggestions, the check says "Ready to publish, with suggestions".

items.title: Send the page for review
items.text:
Contributors, editors and admins all send their pages for review.

  1. Save the page first. The review buttons use the saved page.
  2. Under Review and publishing, you can write a Note for the next person, for example what you changed.
  3. Choose Submit for review. You should see "Sent for review. The editors have been told by email."

The page now waits for review. Every editor and admin gets an e-mail with the page's name and a link to it in the admin panel. A contributor can't change the page while it waits.

items.title: Review, approve and publish a page
items.text:
You need the role editor or admin.

  1. Open the page: choose the link in the e-mail, or find the page under Waiting for review on the Dashboard.
  2. Read the page. View the saved page, at the top, shows it as visitors will see it.
  3. If it needs changes, choose Send back to draft, with a note that says what to change. You should see "Sent back to draft. The writer can change it and send it again."
  4. If it is ready, choose Approve. You should see "Approved. It can be published now."
  5. Choose Publish. You should see "Published. Visitors can see the page now."

If the page still has a problem that stops publishing, Publish is refused, and the list of problems appears at the top with focus on it.

items.title: Look at the published page
items.text:
1. Go to the page's address on the website, for example http://localhost:8080/book-club. The address is shown next to State at the top of the page editor.
  2. You should see the page with its content. It is now also in the website's sitemap and its llms.txt file.

items.title: Take a page off the website
items.text:
1. Open the page in the admin panel.
  2. Choose Unpublish. You should see "Unpublished. Visitors can’t see the page any more; it is a draft again."

The page becomes a draft and goes through review again before it is back on the website.

items.title: Blocks
items.text:
A page's content is a list of blocks, shown one after another. Each kind of block holds one kind of content, such as a heading, some text or a picture. SightPress comes with ten kinds. Add-on modules can add more.

This page lists every kind, its fields and their limits, and what SightPress checks for accessibility. To add, move and remove blocks, see Write and publish a page.

items.title: How blocks are checked
items.text:
• When you save, every block is checked. Every problem is listed at once, at the top of the page, with a link to the field, for example "Heading text: Fill in this field." Nothing is saved until every block is fine.
  • When you publish, SightPress checks the page for accessibility. Problems marked "stops publishing" below must be fixed first. Problems marked "suggestion" don't stop publishing.
  • Files come from the website's media library and must be the right kind, for example a picture for an Image block. Visitors only see files that are published in the media library; a page that uses an unpublished file can't be published.
  • Every block also has a text version, which AI search engines and other readers get as Markdown. See Search and AI visibility.

Fields marked required must be filled in. All the others are optional.

items.title: Heading
items.text:
A heading that starts a part of the page.

Field Limits Heading text (required) Up to 200 characters. Level (required) 2 to 6. Level 2 starts a main part of the page, 3 a part of that, and so on. The page title is the only level 1.
  • Stops publishing: a heading that skips a level, such as a level 4 straight after a level 2.

items.title: Text
items.text:
Formatted text: paragraphs, lists, links and more.

Field Limits Text (required) Up to 100,000 characters, written as HTML.

You can use paragraphs <p>, headings <h2> to <h6>, lists <ul>, <ol> and <li>, links <a href="…">, <strong> and <em>. Quotes, code, abbreviations and description lists work too, and a text or background colour written as style="color: #1a1a1a" or style="background-color: #ffeb3b". Anything else is removed when you save. Scripts, embedded frames and pictures are always removed; use an Image block for pictures. Text pasted from other editors keeps its words.

  • Stops publishing: a link with no text; a level 1 heading or a heading that skips a level; a colour that is too faint to read (a contrast below 4.5 to 1, in light or dark mode); a language code that isn't real.
  • Suggestion: link text that doesn't say where it goes, such as "click here", "read more" or a bare web address.

items.title: Image
items.text:
One picture from the media library.

Field Limits Image (required) A picture from the media library. Alternative text Up to 1,000 characters. What the picture shows, for people who can't see it. The picture is only decoration: screen readers skip it Tick it only for a picture that adds nothing to the page. Caption Up to 2,000 characters. Shown under the picture, for everyone.
  • Stops publishing: no alternative text, when the picture isn't marked as decoration.
  • Suggestion: alternative text that looks like a file name, starts with "image of", or is longer than 250 characters.

items.title: Gallery
items.text:
A set of pictures, shown as a list so that screen readers say how many there are.

Field Limits Pictures (required) 1 to 50 pictures. Each has Picture, Alternative text, the decoration tick box and Caption, as in an Image block. Caption of the gallery Up to 2,000 characters. Shown under all the pictures.

Every picture is checked like an Image block.

items.title: Video
items.text:
A video from the media library, with captions and a transcript. It never starts by itself.

Field Limits Video (required) A video from the media library. Title (required) Up to 200 characters. Names the video for screen readers and search engines. Captions A WebVTT captions file (.vtt) from the media library. Language of the captions A language tag such as en-GB. Leave it empty for the page's language. The video has no speech or important sounds, so it needs no captions A tick box. Poster picture A picture shown before the video plays. Transcript Up to 100,000 characters. Everything said and shown, as text. Shown under the video behind a Transcript button.
  • Stops publishing: a video with speech but no captions; a video marked as having no speech, but with no transcript that describes what it shows.
  • Suggestion: a video without a transcript.

A captions file is a plain text file whose first line is WEBVTT. Upload it to the media library like any other file.

items.title: Audio
items.text:
A sound recording from the media library, with a transcript. It never starts by itself.

Field Limits Audio (required) A sound file from the media library. Title (required) Up to 200 characters. Names the recording for screen readers and search engines. Transcript Up to 100,000 characters. Everything said, as text. Shown under the player behind a Transcript button.
  • Stops publishing: no transcript.

items.title: File download
items.text:
A link to a file from the media library, such as a PDF.

Field Limits File (required) A file from the media library. Link text (required) Up to 200 characters. What the file is, for example "Annual report 2026".

SightPress adds the file's type and size to the link, written for the page's language: "Annual report 2026 (PDF, 2.3 MB)".

  • Suggestion: link text that says nothing on its own, such as "here" or "details".

items.title: Call to action
items.text:
A button that leads somewhere.

Field Limits Button text (required) Up to 80 characters. Say what happens, for example "Book a visit". Link address (required) Up to 2,000 characters. A page of this website, such as /contact, a full address such as https://example.org, or a mailto: or tel: address. Style Primary for the main action of the page, secondary for others.
  • Suggestion: button text that doesn't say what happens, such as "click here".

items.title: Columns
items.text:
Two to four columns side by side on wide screens, one after another on narrow screens and when zoomed in. The columns are read in order: the first column, then the second.

Field Limits Columns (required) 2 to 4 columns. Blocks in each column Up to 50 blocks of any kind except Columns.

Every block in a column is checked as if it were on the page.

items.title: Contact form
items.text:
A form visitors use to send you a message. It has fields for their name, e-mail address and message.

Field Limits Send messages to (required) The e-mail address that gets the messages. It is never shown on the page. Email subject Up to 100 characters. The subject of the e-mails you get. Button text Up to 40 characters. Message after sending Up to 300 characters. The thank-you message visitors see.
  • Messages arrive from the website's own address. Reply to them as usual: the reply goes to the visitor.
  • Spam is kept out without a puzzle: a hidden field that people never see, and at most 5 messages per visitor every 10 minutes.
  • When something is missing, the visitor comes back to the same page with a list of what to fix, which gets focus, and what they typed is kept. After sending, the thank-you message gets focus.
  • The form only works on a published, public page.

items.title: For developers
items.text:
A module adds a kind of block with $registrar->blockTypes()->add(MyBlock::class), a class that implements SightPress\Module\Block\BlockType. Names of other modules' kinds need a vendor prefix, such as acme.event_card.

The fields come from the block's JSON Schema (draft 2020-12). Give every field a title (its label) and a description (its hint). Core enforces only these keywords, and refuses a schema with any other, so no rule is ever skipped without notice: type, properties, required, additionalProperties, enum, minLength, maxLength, pattern, minimum, maximum, items, minItems, maxItems, format and contentMediaType: text/html (rich text, cleaned on save). The formats are link, email, media, media-image, media-video, media-audio, media-document and media-captions.

Core's own kinds are named heading, rich_text, image, gallery, video, audio, file_download, call_to_action, columns and contact_form.

items.title: Command line reference
items.text:
SightPress has a command line tool, bin/sightpress, for the tasks that are done once per website or by whoever runs the installation: creating websites, turning them on and off, and moving them. Everyday work, such as writing pages and inviting people, happens in each website's admin panel.

The tool writes plain sentences, without tables or colours, so that its answers read well with a screen reader. It never shows a database password.

items.title: How to run it
items.text:
With the skeleton running in Docker, start every command from the skeleton folder with docker compose run --rm --no-deps php, for example:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps php bin/sightpress list

You should see every command with one line about what it does. For the details of one command, type bin/sightpress help and its name, for example bin/sightpress help site:create.

Most commands need APP_SECRET to be set (see step 6 of Getting started).

items.title: How commands ask questions
items.text:
If you leave out something a command needs, it asks for it, one question at a time, and also asks the optional questions that have a usual answer. Every command asks the same way:

  • a question that ends with "Press Enter for" and a value takes that value when you just press Enter;
  • a question that lists choices accepts one of them, in capitals or not;
  • a password is not shown as you type it, and is never printed; you type it twice, and if the two are not the same you are asked for it again;
  • some answers are read back in words for you to confirm, for example a language code;
  • a wrong answer is explained and asked again; after 3 wrong answers in a row the command stops and changes nothing;
  • at the end, the command lists your answers and asks "Is all of this right?". Answer no to go through the questions again, with your answers kept: press Enter for each one that was right.

If you give everything on the command line, nothing is asked. Add --no-interaction (or -n) to never be asked: then a missing or wrong value stops the command with a sentence that says what is wrong.

<slug> below is the short name of a website, the one you gave site:create, such as demo.

items.title: site:create
items.text:
site:create [<slug>] [--domain=] [--db= | --db-engine= --db-path= | --db-host= --db-port= --db-name= --db-user= --db-password=]
            [--owner-type=] [--locale=] [--admin-email=] [--admin-first-name=] [--admin-last-name=]
            [--name=] [--timezone=] [--url=] [--create-db] [--with-demo-content] [--without=]

Creates a website: its database tables, its roles, its first admin, six starter pages, its menus and its logo, icon and share image. It prints the first admin's setup code. Nothing is created if something is wrong. Create a website explains every option. --without= names optional features (module ids, separated by commas) the website starts with off.

items.title: site:user:create-admin
items.text:
site:user:create-admin <slug> --email= --first-name= --last-name= [--url=]

Creates an admin on a website and prints the setup code they choose their password with. For an admin who hasn't chosen a password yet, it prints a new code, and the old one stops working. Someone who can already sign in is refused: they use "Forgot your password?" instead.

items.title: Turn websites on and off
items.text:
Command What it does Visitors see site:enable <slug> Turns a website on, so it answers again. Also brings back a deleted website. the website site:disable <slug> Turns a website off for a while. "temporarily unavailable" (503) site:archive <slug> Archives a website. Its data is kept. "gone" (410) site:delete <slug> Deletes a website, softly: it stops answering and its data is kept until site:purge. "not found" (404) site:purge <slug> [--drop-database] Removes a deleted website for good. Its database is kept unless you add --drop-database, which can't be undone. —

Every change is written to the installation's log.

items.title: Look after websites
items.text:
Command What it does site:list Lists the websites: status, domains, language, time zone and database (engine, host and name only). site:migrate <slug> or site:migrate --all Updates a website's database tables after an update of SightPress. --all updates every website that isn't deleted; one failure doesn't stop the others. site:db:change <slug> [--db= or the --db-… parts] [--migrate] Points a disabled website at another database, asked for in parts like in site:create. Nothing is copied: move the data first. The new database must be up to date, or add --migrate. If anything fails, the website keeps its old database. site:seo:check <slug> Checks what search engines will find: titles longer than 60 characters, missing or too long descriptions, pages left out of search and why. Ends with an error when two pages have the same title. See Search and AI visibility.

| system:check | Lists the server's upload and input limits, the largest file of each kind that can be uploaded, and the settings to change. Ends with an error when something must be fixed. Run it with docker compose exec php so it reads the same settings as the website. See Fix upload size limits. |

To move a website to another database:

bin/sightpress site:disable demo
# copy the data to the new database with your database's own tools
bin/sightpress site:db:change demo --db=postgresql://user:password@db.internal:5432/demo
bin/sightpress site:enable demo

items.title: Features
items.text:
Command What it does site:module:list <slug> Lists the website's optional features (modules): id, name and whether each one is on. site:module:enable <slug> <module> Turns a feature on, after updating the website's database for it. Refused while a feature it needs is off. site:module:disable <slug> <module> [--purge-data] Turns a feature off; its data is kept. Refused while a feature that is on needs it. --purge-data also deletes its data, for good.

Features the installation set in config/tenant.php (modules.locked) can't be changed. See Turn features on or off.

items.title: Site search
items.text:
Command What it does site:search:reindex <slug> [--locale=<locale>] Builds the website's search index again from its published pages, in every language or one. site:search:status <slug> How many pages the search index holds in each language, when it last changed, and whether it is waiting to be rebuilt. site:search <slug> <words> [--locale=<locale>] [--members] Searches the website the way a visitor would (--members: as someone signed in) and lists the first results.

They refuse a website with search turned off. See Search your website.

items.title: Analytics
items.text:
Command What it does site:analytics:report <slug> [--from=YYYY-MM-DD] [--to=YYYY-MM-DD] [--report=<name>\|all] [--format=table\|csv\|json] Shows the website's analytics, the last 30 days by default. Reports: summary, daily, pages, sources, languages, devices, searches, searches-without-results, not-found, bots. Warns when the hourly roll-up hasn't run for two hours. site:analytics:purge <slug> [--before=YYYY-MM-DD] Deletes the figures from before a day; without --before, those older than the website keeps them.

They refuse a website with analytics turned off. See See who visits your website.

items.title: AI assistant
items.text:
Command What it does site:assistant:set <slug> --provider=<id> --model=<model> [--base-url=<address>] [--key-stdin] Chooses the AI service (anthropic, openai, mistral or openai_compatible) and model. With --key-stdin it reads the API key from standard input, so it never appears in the shell history: printf %s "$KEY" \| bin/sightpress site:assistant:set …. site:assistant:test <slug> Sends a tiny request and says whether the service answered. site:assistant:usage <slug> [--month=YYYY-MM] Shows the tokens used this month (or another), per task, and the budget. site:assistant:disable <slug> [--remove-key] Turns the assistant off for the website, and removes its key with --remove-key. assistant:ask <slug> "<question>" Asks the assistant a question from the console.

They refuse a website with the assistant turned off; turn it on with site:module:enable <slug> assistant. See Use the AI assistant.

items.title: Branding
items.text:
Command What it does site:branding:set <slug> [--logo=] [--logo-alt=] [--icon=] [--share-image=] [--share-image-alt=] Uses picture files for the logo (SVG, PNG, JPEG or WebP, from 1:1 to 8:1 wide), the icon (a square PNG, JPEG or WebP of at least 512 × 512 pixels) or the share image (PNG, JPEG or WebP of 1200 × 630 pixels, or larger with the same proportions). The -alt options say what the picture shows, for screen readers; the default is the website's name. site:branding:reset <slug> [--logo] [--icon] [--share-image] Goes back to the generated logo, icon or share image; all three unless you name some. site:branding:regenerate <slug> Makes the generated pictures again from the website's name, for example after renaming it. Uploaded pictures stay.

Admins can do the same in the admin panel, under Branding.

items.title: The site registry
items.text:
The installation keeps its list of websites in config/sites.php, with each database address encrypted with APP_SECRET.

Command What it does site:registry:check Checks the file, and that every database address can be read with this APP_SECRET, and says what to fix. site:registry:upgrade Upgrades the file to the format this version of SightPress reads.

Each change to the file keeps the previous version as config/sites.php.bak.

items.title: theme:validate
items.text:
theme:validate [<path>]

Checks a theme's colour contrast, in light and dark mode and with and without more contrast, and its base font size, against WCAG 2.2 AA, and says what to fix. Without a path, it checks the active theme. It ends with an error when a check fails.

items.title: Database addresses
items.text:
--db takes the address (DSN) of a database:

Engine Example SQLite (a file) sqlite:////app/sites/demo.sqlite MySQL mysql://user:password@mysql:3306/demo MariaDB mariadb://user:password@mariadb:3306/demo PostgreSQL postgresql://user:password@postgres:5432/demo

A SQLite file and its folder are created when missing. On the other engines the database must exist, unless you add --create-db to site:create and the database user is allowed to create databases. To start a database server on your computer, see Start a database server.

items.title: Roles and permissions
items.text: Everyone who signs in to a SightPress website has one role. A role is a set of permissions: each permission lets a person do one thing, such as publish pages. Each website keeps its own people and roles, so someone can be an editor on one website and a contributor on another.

items.title: The four roles
items.text:
Every new website has these roles. The admin panel describes each one in the same words when you invite someone or change their role.

Role What the admin panel says In short Admin Can do everything, including inviting people, changing roles and site settings. Runs the website. Editor Can write, review and publish any page, and invite contributors. Looks after the content. Contributor Can write pages and send them for review, but not publish them. Writes. Member Can sign in and read the site, but not use the admin panel. Reads.

The admin and member roles can't be renamed or deleted. The member role never has any permission. Every new website has one admin: the person named when it was created (see Create a website).

items.title: What each role can do
items.text:
Permission What it lets you do Admin Editor Contributor Member Use the admin panel Sign in to the admin panel. yes yes yes no Create pages Start new pages. yes yes yes no Edit own pages Change pages they wrote. yes yes yes no Edit any page Change pages anyone wrote. yes yes no no Submit pages for review Send a page to the editors. yes yes yes no Publish pages Approve, publish and unpublish pages. yes yes no no Archive pages Take pages off the site and keep them. yes yes no no Delete pages Delete pages for good. yes yes no no Upload media Add pictures, video, audio and files. yes yes yes no Publish media Make uploaded files public. yes yes no no Manage menus Change the main and footer menus. yes yes no no Invite people Invite people to the site with a role they are allowed to give. yes yes no no Manage users Change the role of any user, and deactivate accounts. yes no no no Manage roles Create roles and change what they allow. yes no no no Manage site settings Change the site's name, profile, branding and other settings. yes no no no Manage features Turn the site's optional features on and off, and delete their data (how). yes no no no Apply themes Choose the site's theme. yes no no no View the audit log See who changed what, and when. yes no no no View analytics See how many people visit the site, what they read and where they come from (how). yes yes no no Manage analytics Choose how long analytics are kept, and delete them. yes no no no Use the AI assistant Ask the AI assistant for suggestions, which they check before using (how).
